questions.text: When you type a question into ChatGPT, what is the tool actually doing?

options.text: Generating new text in real time by predicting a plausible, relevant sequence of words.
Looking the answer up in a database of verified responses.
Retrieving the most relevant passages from the books and articles it was trained on and quoting them.
Consulting notes it saved from your previous conversations.

questions.explanation: The lesson describes ChatGPT as generating text rather than searching a database of answers, and this is precisely what explains both its fluency and its capacity to sound confident while being wrong.

questions.text: Which of these does the lesson recommend as starter workflows for a teacher new to ChatGPT?

options.text: Producing a first-draft lesson outline that you then adjust for pacing, examples and objectives.
Turning one short text into several versions at different reading levels for a mixed-ability class.
Rewriting your own material — a parent letter or a set of classroom instructions — for clarity or a particular audience.
Pasting your class list so that materials can be personalised for each named student.
Asking it to confirm which facts in a textbook chapter are correct.

questions.explanation: Lesson outlines, differentiated versions of a text and rewriting your own material are among the four starter workflows the lesson proposes. Entering student names is ruled out on data-protection grounds, and the tool cannot be used as a fact-checker because it does not know whether its own output is correct.

questions.text: What does the lesson recommend doing whenever a prompt produces a genuinely useful result?

options.text: Save it with a short note about when it worked, so it becomes part of a personal library you adapt later.
Run it several more times to check that the output stays stable.
Ask ChatGPT to remember it and apply it in future conversations.
Publish it so that colleagues in other schools can reuse it directly.

questions.explanation: Building a personal prompt library is one of the two deliberate choices the lesson names for turning a first try into regular practice: next time you need similar output you adapt a prompt that already worked rather than starting from scratch.

questions.text: Anything typed into ChatGPT is sent to OpenAI's servers and may be used to improve their models unless you opt out, so material that would normally identify a student should be anonymised first.
questions.explanation: The lesson makes both points directly and advises replacing names with "Student A", "Student B" and removing any detail that could identify a real person: treat the tool as an unsecured channel, since everything you type leaves your device.
